sections.h2: Who keeps property records in Seminole County, Florida?
sections.html:
The Seminole County Clerk of the Circuit Court and Comptroller keeps them, in a single series called the Official Records.

The clerk's Official Records page lists the kinds of documents held there: deeds, mortgages, notices of commencement, liens, declarations of condominium, final judgments, military discharges, probate documents, satisfactions of mortgage, plats and maps. Florida's county offices divide the work, and it helps to know which one answers which question.

  • Clerk: recorded deeds, mortgages, liens and plats; also runs tax deed sales.
  • Property appraiser: ownership on the tax roll, assessed value and exemptions.
  • Tax collector: tax bills, payments, installment plans and delinquent accounts.

Each of the three is a separately elected county office under Florida's constitution, so a record you need may live in only one of them.

sections.h2: How do you record a document with the Seminole County Clerk?
sections.html:
You can bring it in, mail it with the fees and a self-addressed stamped envelope, or send it through an electronic recording portal.

The Official Records department is at 1750 E. Lake Mary Blvd., Sanford, FL 32773, phone 407-665-4405, according to the clerk's page. Recording fees and any documentary stamp tax are due when the document is recorded. The clerk says electronically submitted documents are typically recorded within 24 to 72 hours, and the image can be pulled from the Official Records page once recorded.

The clerk lists four approved eRecording vendors: CSC eRecording, eRecording Partners Network, Hopdox and Simplifile. Suggested practices include 300 DPI scans, TIFF or PDF format, 8 by 11 pages, party names indexed as last name then first name, and no more than 15 documents per receipt.

Some documents cannot be sent electronically and must be mailed or hand delivered: a notice of contest of lien, notice of contest of bond, notice of homestead, a transfer of liens to security by bond or cash, a transfer of judgment, and a notice of marketable title when a certificate of service is required.

sections.h2: What does recording cost in Seminole County?
sections.html:
The clerk's posted sheet lists $10.00 for the first page and $8.50 for each additional page.

That sheet also prints the stamp and tax lines that ride along with a deed or mortgage, plus service charges for copies and searches. Under Florida law, the deed stamp tax rate is 70 cents per $100 of consideration, and a mortgage carries 35 cents per $100 of the amount secured. The clerk's sheet shows the same deed and mortgage rates and adds an intangible tax on a mortgage at 20 cents per $100.

sections.h2: Why does Florida's recording statute matter to a Seminole County seller?
sections.html:
Because the statute tells the clerk what to record and open to the public, and sets the charge.

Chapter 28 makes the clerk the recorder, and a deed of land must be written and signed in front of two subscribing witnesses under section 689.01, with witnessing allowed by audio-video technology. If your deed has a defect such as a missing witness, the title company will catch it, but fixing it takes time. Quitclaim deeds, deeds in lieu of foreclosure and contracts for deed are all taxable documents according to the Department of Revenue. Spousal homestead deeds where the only consideration is a mortgage, and divorce deeds for a marital home, are exempt.

A personal representative's deed under a probated will is listed as not taxable, but the Department of Revenue says there is no general exemption for transfers made for estate planning.

sections.h2: How are Seminole County property taxes billed and collected?
sections.html:
The tax collector bills in November and the early-payment discount runs 4 percent that month, then 3, 2 and 1 percent through February.

The tax collector's site says taxes become delinquent on April 1, after which they are listed on the county website and advertising and collection fees are added. Installment plans are offered with an application, and a payment missed under the plan is treated as delinquent on April 1. Seminole's site also says a discount period ending on a weekend or holiday extends to the next working day when payment is delivered to a qualifying location.

Value is set January 1 and exemptions filed by March 1 with the property appraiser. A homestead exemption up to $50,000 applies: the first $25,000 to all taxes and an added amount to non-school taxes on value over $50,000. After a sale, the next owner's assessment resets to just value the following January 1.

sections.h2: What happens at a Seminole County tax deed sale?
sections.html:
The clerk conducts the sale and issues the tax deed to the high bidder.

The clerk's page explains that a tax certificate holder applies for a tax deed through the tax collector, that no court case is filed, and that no court order is issued for the sale. The page warns that tax deed properties are sold on a buyer beware basis and that a tax deed does not warrant clear and marketable title. The clerk's tax deed department answers questions at taxdeeds@seminoleclerk.org, and auction files and the calendar are online.

Under Florida law, the certificate holder may apply two years after April 1 of the issuance year, and the buyer pays 5 percent or $200, whichever is greater, as a nonrefundable deposit, with full payment due within 24 hours excluding weekends and holidays. An owner with delinquent taxes should settle them with the tax collector before the sale to protect the property.

sections.h2: What should a Seminole County owner check before selling?
sections.html:
Check the record chain, then the bills, then the exemptions.

  • Search the Official Records online for your deed and any recorded mortgage, lien or judgment.
  • Confirm that satisfied mortgages show a recorded satisfaction.
  • Ask the property appraiser to confirm your exemptions and parcel data.
  • Ask the tax collector whether the current year is paid.
  • List all names exactly as they appear on the deed for the new instrument.

The clerk reminds users to search every spelling variation of a name, since the index is only as accurate as what was filed. Cities in the county such as Winter Springs follow the same county recording process, so the steps here apply there too.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Seminole County?
faqs.a: With the Seminole County Clerk's Official Records department at 1750 E. Lake Mary Blvd., Sanford. You can also use an approved eRecording vendor.

faqs.q: How much does recording cost in Seminole County?
faqs.a: The clerk's sheet lists $10.00 for the first page and $8.50 for each added page. Deed stamp tax is separate at 70 cents per $100.

faqs.q: Can I send any document through eRecording?
faqs.a: No. The clerk lists documents that must be mailed or hand delivered, including a notice of homestead and a notice of contest of lien.

faqs.q: Who runs tax deed sales in Seminole County?
faqs.a: The clerk conducts them under Chapter 197, Florida Statutes. No court case is filed for the sale.

faqs.q: When do Seminole County property taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: On April 1. The tax collector lists a 4 percent discount for November payment, falling to 1 percent in February.
